body:
# UK GLP-1 Dosing: 4 week steps to cut side effects and protect muscle

![GLP-1 dosing title card illustration](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791293523083_GLP-1-dosing-title-card-illustration.jpeg)

GLP-1 medicines are started at low doses and escalated at manufacturer-recommended intervals to a tolerated maintenance dose. This guide covers semaglutide (oral and injectable), tirzepatide, liraglutide, exenatide and dulaglutide, with the schedules used in UK prescribing. Always confirm your exact dose with your prescriber, and never start or continue any of these medicines during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - Most GLP-1 medicines require minimum four-week intervals at each dose before escalation, except liraglutide, which allows one-week steps.
> - Switching between form factors, such as injectable and oral semaglutide, alters absorption and should only be managed with clinical guidance.
> - Gastrointestinal side effects like nausea and vomiting are common during dose increases and can be mitigated by hydration, diet adjustments, and careful monitoring.
> - Missed-dose rules depend on the product and formulation: weekly semaglutide injections and daily semaglutide tablets have different instructions. Follow your own leaflet and never double doses to compensate.
> - These medicines are contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and effective contraception is advised during treatment.

***

## Table of Contents

- [Dosing by medication: semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide and more](#dosing-by-medication-semaglutide-tirzepatide-liraglutide-and-more)
- [Titration schedules at a glance](#titration-schedules-at-a-glance)
- [Taking GLP-1 medicines correctly day to day](#taking-glp-1-medicines-correctly-day-to-day)
- [Side effects, interactions and when to get urgent help](#side-effects-interactions-and-when-to-get-urgent-help)
- [Missed doses, changing your schedule and stopping safely](#missed-doses-changing-your-schedule-and-stopping-safely)
- [What structured support adds to safe dosing](#what-structured-support-adds-to-safe-dosing)
- [Our take: titration charts are a starting point, not the plan](#our-take-titration-charts-are-a-starting-point-not-the-plan)
- [Getting clinically governed support for your GLP-1 journey](#getting-clinically-governed-support-for-your-glp-1-journey)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Sources](#sources)

## Dosing by medication: semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide and more

Each GLP-1 medicine has its own titration pattern, and the step sizes, intervals and maximum doses differ enough that mixing them up is a genuine risk. Here is what the product information sets out for the medicines most commonly prescribed.

- **Semaglutide tablets:** Wegovy tablets for weight management and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes are different products. [MHRA guidance for Wegovy tablets](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/first-glp-1-tablet-for-weight-loss-approved-in-the-uk) starts at 1.5 mg once daily, then 4 mg, 9 mg and 25 mg at monthly steps. Rybelsus has its own strengths and instructions; do not transfer its schedule to Wegovy. Follow the prescription and leaflet for the exact product, and arrange any switch with your prescriber.

For a direct head-to-head on how semaglutide and liraglutide differ in practice, our [Wegovy vs Saxenda comparison](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/comparisons/medications/wegovy-vs-saxenda) walks through the trade-offs.

## Titration schedules at a glance

Use this as a quick reference only. Your prescriber's instructions and the medicine's own product information always take precedence over any chart.

Switching between formulations, such as moving from injectable to oral semaglutide, can change how predictably the medicine is absorbed, so this isn't something to manage without clinical input.

## Taking GLP-1 medicines correctly day to day

Getting the practical details right cuts down on side effects and wasted doses.

1. **Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus):** take it fasted, with no more than 120 mL of water, and wait at least 30 minutes before eating, drinking anything else, or taking other oral medicines.
2. **Weekly injectables:** pick a day that suits your routine and stick to it; if you need to change the day, leave at least 72 hours between doses.
3. **Injection sites:** the abdomen, thigh and upper arm all work, and rotating between them reduces irritation at any one spot.
4. **Pen handling:** keep spare needles on hand, never reuse a needle, and follow the priming steps in the device instructions each time.
5. **Persistent nausea or vomiting:** this is a reason to hold off on the next dose increase and speak to your clinician rather than push through.

**Pro Tip:** *During a dose increase, eat smaller, plainer meals for the first few days and keep strongly flavoured drinks like coffee away from mealtimes, it tends to make nausea noticeably more manageable.*

## Side effects, interactions and when to get urgent help

Gastrointestinal side effects are the most common complaint with every GLP-1 medicine on this list, and they tend to cluster around dose increases rather than staying constant.

**More than 1 in 10 patients report gastrointestinal side effects** such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, according to MHRA drug safety guidance. The same guidance flags dehydration as a real risk during flare-ups, so keeping fluids up matters more than people expect.

- **Dehydration:** severe or persistent vomiting needs medical review, not just fluids at home.
- **Hypoglycaemia:** combining a GLP-1 with insulin or a sulphonylurea raises the risk of low blood sugar; [Diabetes UK guidance](https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/treatments/tablets-and-medication/glp-1) notes that doses of those other medicines may need reducing, alongside closer glucose monitoring.
- **Pancreatitis warning signs:** severe, persistent abdominal pain that spreads to the back warrants urgent assessment, not a wait-and-see approach.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding:** these medicines are not used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding; effective contraception is advised, and treatment should stop if pregnancy is planned or confirmed.

Our [guide to GLP-1 side effects](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/glp1-side-effects) covers nausea and constipation management in more detail, including when symptoms cross the line into needing medical attention.

## Missed doses, changing your schedule and stopping safely

Each medicine has its own rule for a missed dose, and guessing is riskier than it sounds.

- **Semaglutide (injectable):** take the missed dose within 5 days if you remember in time; beyond that, skip it and resume your normal schedule.
- **Tirzepatide:** the window is shorter, within 4 days; after that, skip and wait for the next scheduled dose.
- **Liraglutide (daily):** follow the specific missed-dose window in the product information and never double up to make up for a skipped day.
- **Changing your injection day:** leave a minimum of 72 hours between doses when shifting to a new weekly slot.
- **Stopping treatment:** this is a decision for you and your prescriber together, particularly if you have diabetes, since stopping can affect blood glucose control. Our article on [stopping GLP-1 treatment](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/stopping-glp1) covers what to expect afterwards, including appetite and weight changes.

## What structured support adds to safe dosing

Following a titration schedule correctly is only part of the picture. What we see matter just as much in practice is protecting muscle and staying properly hydrated while your body adjusts, especially in the first few weeks of any dose increase.

Simple measures go a long way: enough protein at each meal, a couple of sessions of resistance training a week, and deliberate fluid intake around dose days rather than only when thirst kicks in. We cover the detail in our pieces on [preventing GLP-1 muscle loss](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/glp-1-muscle-loss) and [practical steps for men on GLP-1 medicines](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/muscle-on-glp1). Where side effects are getting in the way of eating or sleeping properly, that's the point to flag it with a clinician rather than quietly struggling through an escalation.

![Four priorities for safer GLP-1 support](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791293511902_Four-priorities-for-safer-GLP-1-support.jpeg)

## Our take: titration charts are a starting point, not the plan

The dosing numbers matter, but they're the easy part. What tends to get underrated is everything around the injection itself: whether you're eating enough protein to hold onto muscle, whether you're drinking enough water on the days nausea hits hardest, and whether you've actually told anyone that a dose increase is coming so you can plan around it.

![Our take: titration charts are a starting point, not the plan — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791293568706_Our-take-titration-charts-are-a-starting-point-not-the-plan-overview-diagram.jpeg)

Conventional advice often treats titration as a mechanical process, follow the chart, increase on schedule, done. In practice, the right pace for you depends on how your body responds at each step, not just how many weeks have passed. Tolerating 1 mg of semaglutide badly is a legitimate reason to pause an increase, not push through it because the calendar says so.

If we had to pick one priority, it's this: treat side effects as information, not an inconvenience to tolerate. Persistent nausea, fatigue or GI upset is your body telling you the current dose needs more time, and that's worth listening to before chasing the next step up.

> *— Matt O’Brien*

## Getting clinically governed support for your GLP-1 journey

SHIFT provides general information and free practical support through My Timber, Grub, Fit and Life Back. These resources do not replace a clinical assessment or medicine review. Prescribing, dispensing, dose changes and clinical monitoring remain the responsibility of your appropriately regulated healthcare provider. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while its regulated treatment partner is not commissioned.

For a medicine assessment, review or symptoms, contact your own prescribing service. My Timber check-ins are practical self-tracking and are not clinical monitoring.

## FAQ

### What is the correct starting dose for semaglutide?

The starting dose depends on the named medicine, formulation and indication. Weekly Wegovy injections start at 0.25 mg once weekly for four weeks. For Wegovy tablets used for weight management, the authorised starting dose is 1.5 mg once daily. Rybelsus is a diabetes product with its own instructions; do not use its schedule for Wegovy tablets. Follow your own prescription and product leaflet.

### How quickly can you increase a GLP-1 dose?

Most GLP-1 medicines require a minimum of four weeks at each dose before increasing, with liraglutide being the exception at one week per step. Increasing faster than the product information allows raises the risk of severe nausea and vomiting.

### What happens if you miss a weekly GLP-1 injection?

For semaglutide, you can take the missed dose within 5 days of the scheduled time; beyond that, skip it and wait for your next planned dose. Tirzepatide's window is shorter, within 4 days, after which you should also skip rather than double up.

### Can you take GLP-1 medicines while pregnant?

No, GLP-1 medicines including semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide are not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Effective contraception is advised while on treatment, and anyone planning a pregnancy should speak to their prescriber about stopping beforehand.

### What is the maximum dose of tirzepatide?

The maximum licensed dose of tirzepatide is 15 mg once weekly, reached by increasing from a 2.5 mg starting dose in 2.5 mg steps no sooner than every four weeks, as set out in MHRA dosing guidance. Not everyone needs to reach the top dose, many people reach a good response at 5 mg or 10 mg.

# GLP-1 constipation: practical steps and when to get help

![Illustrated title card for GLP-1 constipation](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791376501531_Illustrated-title-card-for-GLP-1-constipation.jpeg)

GLP-1 medicines commonly slow digestion, and constipation is one of the most reported side effects during treatment. If you're dealing with it now, the two things to try first are simple: drink more fluids and add fibre gradually while staying active. Most cases are mild and settle with time, but severe abdominal pain or vomiting needs urgent medical attention.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - Drink regularly and increase fibre gradually. Follow any prescribed fluid restriction or dietary advice; ask a pharmacist or clinician if unsure.
> - When lifestyle changes fail, start with bulk forming laxatives if fibre intake is low; macrogol is an osmotic option that may take a few days.
> - Seek urgent care for severe, persistent abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, fever, or inability to pass wind or stool, especially if symptoms worsen rapidly.
> - Symptoms often ease over weeks after starting or increasing a dose; ask your prescriber about slower increases if discomfort persists beyond a few weeks.
> - Tell your surgical team before general anesthesia or deep sedation that you take these medicines; delayed stomach emptying can raise aspiration risk despite fasting.

***

## Table of Contents

- [Why GLP-1 medicines cause constipation](#why-glp-1-medicines-cause-constipation)
- [Preventing constipation: daily habits that help](#preventing-constipation-daily-habits-that-help)
- [Safe laxative use if diet and lifestyle aren't enough](#safe-laxative-use-if-diet-and-lifestyle-arent-enough)
- [Red flags: when constipation needs urgent attention](#red-flags-when-constipation-needs-urgent-attention)
- [What to expect over time and during dose escalation](#what-to-expect-over-time-and-during-dose-escalation)
- [What we focus on with men managing this side effect](#what-we-focus-on-with-men-managing-this-side-effect)
- [Telling your surgical or anaesthetic team about GLP-1 use](#telling-your-surgical-or-anaesthetic-team-about-glp-1-use)
- [Food choices and meal timing that help beyond fibre](#food-choices-and-meal-timing-that-help-beyond-fibre)
- [How constipation risk varies between GLP-1 medicines](#how-constipation-risk-varies-between-glp-1-medicines)
- [Managing constipation that doesn't go away](#managing-constipation-that-doesnt-go-away)
- [Constipation, treatment adherence and staying on track](#constipation-treatment-adherence-and-staying-on-track)
- [Our take: the advice that actually moves the needle](#our-take-the-advice-that-actually-moves-the-needle)
- [Support if GLP-1 side effects are getting in the way](#support-if-glp-1-side-effects-are-getting-in-the-way)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Sources](#sources)

## Why GLP-1 medicines cause constipation

GLP-1 medicines work partly by slowing gastric emptying, the process by which food moves from your stomach into your small intestine. This slowing effect extends further down the digestive tract too, so food moves through your intestines more slowly than usual. The result is often firmer, less frequent stools.

There's a second factor at play. These medicines reduce appetite, which means you naturally eat less. Less food means less bulk moving through your gut, and if your fibre intake drops along with your overall intake, your bowel has even less to work with.

Constipation tends to show up most strongly when you start treatment or shortly after a dose increase. This pattern fits with how GLP-1 receptor agonists work, since gastrointestinal side effects are more common during dose escalation and tend to ease as your body adjusts over the following weeks. Knowing this timing helps: a rough patch after a dose step-up is common and often temporary, not necessarily a sign that something has gone wrong.

## Preventing constipation: daily habits that help

Prevention works better than treatment here, and the habits that help are mostly about consistency rather than anything complicated.

Drink regularly and increase fibre gradually. If you have been advised to restrict fluids or follow a particular diet, follow your healthcare team’s instructions. [NHS guidance on constipation](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/constipation/) explains self-care and when to ask a pharmacist or GP for advice.

[Fibre is the other pillar](https://nutrilike.es/probioticos-para-colon-irritable-cuales-funcionan-y-como-elegir-el-adecuado). The same NHS guidance points to around 30 grams a day as a sensible target, but the increase needs to happen slowly over several weeks rather than all at once, since a sudden jump can cause bloating and discomfort. Good sources include:

- Oats, wholemeal bread and brown rice for everyday staples.
- Fruit and vegetables, aiming for a variety across the week.
- Psyllium husk or similar supplements if food sources alone aren't enough.

Movement matters too. A short walk after meals supports digestion, and keeping a loose routine, such as trying a bowel movement after breakfast when your gut is naturally more active, trains your body over time. Don't delay when you feel the urge; putting it off regularly makes constipation more likely.

**Pro Tip:** *Add one extra portion of fibre a week, such as a handful of oats or an extra piece of fruit, and pair every increase with a glass of water to help it move through without bloating.*

## Safe laxative use if diet and lifestyle aren't enough

When lifestyle changes aren't quite doing the job, laxatives offer a safe next step, provided you follow a sensible order and know what to expect.

NHS guidance recommends starting with bulk-forming laxatives if you're not getting enough fibre from food, though these need plenty of fluid to work properly and aren't always the right first choice if your constipation feels severe. Osmotic laxatives such as macrogol are often favoured because they draw water into the bowel and soften stool, and they typically take a few days to work, according to NHS guidance.

For quicker relief, stimulant laxatives are an option:

- Stimulant laxatives typically work within 6 to 12 hours, making them useful if you need relief overnight.
- Stool softeners can ease straining without the stimulant effect.
- Glycerol suppositories act as a rescue option when oral laxatives haven't worked quickly enough.

Local NHS formulary guidance on [managing constipation](https://www.cheshireandmerseysideformulary.nhs.uk/docs/files/West%20Cheshire%20-%20Management%20of%20Constipation%20in%20Adults%20v2.0%20-%20July%202020.pdf?UNLID=423672992202661261850) sets out this stepwise approach, moving from bulk-forming to osmotic to stimulant agents depending on response. Avoid relying on stimulant laxatives long-term without medical advice, since overuse can disrupt your body's normal rhythm and, in some cases, affect electrolyte balance. If constipation persists beyond a few weeks despite trying these steps, it's time to speak to your GP or prescriber.

## Red flags: when constipation needs urgent attention

Most constipation on GLP-1 medicines is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, but a few symptoms mean you should act quickly rather than wait it out.

Seek urgent medical help if you experience severe, persistent abdominal pain, particularly if it spreads to your back. [Gov](https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/glp-1-receptor-agonists-and-dual-glp-1-slash-gip-receptor-agonists-strengthened-warnings-on-acute-pancreatitis-including-necrotising-and-fatal-cases) has strengthened warnings around acute pancreatitis, including rare but serious cases, and this kind of pain pattern is one of the signs that needs prompt assessment rather than home management.

Other red flags include repeated vomiting, fever, or an inability to pass wind or stool at all, which can point to a bowel obstruction. Contact your GP or NHS 111 for guidance on the right level of care, or go to A&E if symptoms are severe or rapidly worsening. If you suspect you've had an adverse reaction to your medicine, you can also report it through the Yellow Card scheme, which helps the MHRA track safety signals across the population.

![Urgent constipation warning signs and care routes](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791376497812_Urgent-constipation-warning-signs-and-care-routes.jpeg)

## What to expect over time and during dose escalation

Gastrointestinal side effects, including constipation, are most noticeable when you start a GLP-1 medicine or step up your dose, and they typically ease over the following weeks as your body adapts. This pattern is common enough that prescribers often plan for it, sometimes slowing the pace of dose increases if side effects are proving difficult.

During escalation phases, it's worth reinforcing the basics: extra fluids, steady fibre, regular movement. If you stop treatment altogether, your digestion will likely return towards its previous pattern over time, though this varies from person to person. Ongoing support, rather than a one-off fix, tends to make these transitions easier to manage.

## What we focus on with men managing this side effect

We see constipation come up often in conversations with men starting GLP-1 treatment, and the practical fixes tend to matter more than anything complicated. Simple hydration routines, small fibre swaps built into meals you already eat, and a consistent time to try the toilet each day make a real difference for most people.

Clinical review and day-to-day lifestyle support work best together rather than as separate tracks. When side effects do show up, having both strands in place, medical oversight alongside practical, everyday adjustments, means problems get caught and addressed early rather than left to become a bigger issue.

## Telling your surgical or anaesthetic team about GLP-1 use

If you're due to have surgery or any procedure involving general anaesthesia or deep sedation, it's important to mention that you're taking a GLP-1 medicine, even if your appointment feels unrelated to your digestion or weight.

GOV.UK safety guidance explains that because these medicines slow gastric emptying, there's a potential risk of pulmonary aspiration during anaesthesia, meaning stomach contents could be inhaled into the lungs if your stomach hasn't emptied as expected. This can happen even after a standard fasting period, since delayed emptying means food may still be present in your stomach longer than usual.

Before any planned procedure, let your surgical team, anaesthetist, and even your dentist if sedation is involved, know which GLP-1 medicine you're taking and your current dose. They may adjust fasting instructions or take extra precautions as a result. This is a straightforward conversation to have, and it's far better to mention it upfront than to assume it isn't relevant.

## Food choices and meal timing that help beyond fibre

Fibre gets most of the attention, but a few other dietary adjustments can ease constipation without adding bulk you might struggle to manage on a reduced appetite.

Certain foods have a reputation for helping things along more directly. Patient guidance from [Cambridge University Hospitals on bowel function](https://www.cuh.nhs.uk/patient-information/improving-bowel-function-in-constipation/) points to prunes and kiwifruit as helpful additions, since both have evidence behind them for increasing stool frequency, even in smaller quantities than you might expect.

Meal timing matters too, particularly when appetite is low. Eating smaller, more regular meals rather than skipping meals and then eating one large one tends to be gentler on a slower digestive system. Very fatty or heavy meals can sit longer in a stomach that's already emptying slowly, so lighter, more balanced plates generally sit more comfortably. Warm drinks with breakfast, such as tea or warm water, can also help stimulate the natural gut reflex that many people experience first thing in the morning.

If constipation feels linked to broader side effects such as nausea, it's worth reading more on [managing GLP-1 side effects](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/glp1-side-effects) together, since the same meal-timing adjustments often ease both.

![Food choices and meal timing that help beyond fibre — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791376558607_Food-choices-and-meal-timing-that-help-beyond-fibre-overview-diagram.jpeg)

## How constipation risk varies between GLP-1 medicines

Constipation appears as a common gastrointestinal side effect across GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 medicines, though individual experience varies depending on which medicine and dose you're taking. Product information for tirzepatide lists constipation among its common gastrointestinal effects, and rates tend to be higher during dose escalation before settling for most people.

The exact way each medicine affects your gut can differ slightly depending on its formulation and dosing schedule, including how quickly doses step up and how often you inject. If you find constipation particularly difficult on one medicine, this is worth discussing with your prescriber, since adjusting the pace of dose increases or switching formulations within the same class is sometimes an option. This isn't something to manage alone; it's a conversation for your clinical team, who can weigh your specific situation against the available options.

## Managing constipation that doesn't go away

For most people, constipation on GLP-1 medicines eases within weeks as the body adjusts, but a smaller number of people find it persists longer term. If that's your experience, it's worth stepping back and reviewing the full picture rather than just adding another laxative.

Local NHS guidance on [managing constipation in adults](https://bswpartnership.nhs.uk/medicines/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2021/08/BSW-Guidance-on-the-Management-of-Constipation-in-Adults-v1.0.pdf) recommends checking for other contributing factors, since other medicines, reduced activity, or changes in diet can all compound the effect of GLP-1 treatment on your bowel. A GP review can rule these out and adjust your approach accordingly.

Persistent constipation sometimes calls for a longer-term laxative plan rather than occasional rescue doses, used under medical guidance rather than on an ad hoc basis. Keeping a simple record of your bowel habits, fluid intake and fibre intake for a couple of weeks can also help your GP spot patterns and tailor advice more precisely than a single conversation would allow.

## Constipation, treatment adherence and staying on track

Uncomfortable side effects are one of the most common reasons people consider stopping GLP-1 treatment early, and constipation is no exception. When a side effect feels unmanageable, it's tempting to quietly reduce doses, skip injections, or stop altogether rather than raise it with your prescriber.

The better path is usually to treat constipation as a manageable, expected part of early treatment rather than a reason to give up. Proactive hydration and fibre habits from day one reduce the chances of symptoms becoming severe enough to disrupt your routine. When side effects do intensify, particularly around dose increases, flagging this early with your prescriber opens up options like slower titration, which keeps you moving towards your goals without the discomfort derailing progress. If you've paused or stopped a medicine because of side effects, it's worth reading about [what happens when you stop GLP-1 treatment](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/stopping-glp1) before deciding on next steps, since restarting or adjusting your approach is often possible with the right support.

## Our take: the advice that actually moves the needle

Most advice on GLP-1 constipation reads like a long list of equally weighted tips, which does readers a disservice. In our view, two things matter far more than the rest: getting fluid intake right from day one, and treating fibre increases as a gradual process rather than a single fix. Most of the discomfort we hear about comes from people either under-hydrating or adding too much fibre too quickly, which backfires into bloating rather than relief.

The conventional advice also underplays how closely constipation ties into whether people stick with treatment at all. A side effect that feels unmanageable in week two can quietly become the reason someone stops in week six, long before they've given the medicine a fair chance to work. We'd rather see people flag discomfort early and adjust pace, diet and hydration together, than struggle in silence and lose momentum on a treatment that's otherwise working for them.

> *— Matt O’Brien*

## Support if GLP-1 side effects are getting in the way

SHIFT provides general information and free practical support through My Timber, Grub, Fit and Life Back. These resources do not replace a clinical assessment or medicine review. Prescribing, dispensing, dose changes and clinical monitoring remain the responsibility of your appropriately regulated healthcare provider. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while its regulated treatment partner is not commissioned.

If side effects persist, contact your pharmacist or prescriber. For severe symptoms, follow the urgent-care advice above rather than waiting for a SHIFT reply.

## FAQ

### Why does GLP-1 make you constipated?

GLP-1 medicines slow gastric emptying and intestinal transit, meaning food moves through your digestive system more slowly than usual. Reduced appetite also means less food bulk and often less fibre intake, which together increase the likelihood of constipation, particularly during dose increases.

### Why am I so constipated after losing weight?

Weight loss itself can reduce constipation risk if it comes with more activity and better hydration, but rapid weight loss alongside reduced food intake, as often happens on GLP-1 medicines, can mean less fibre and fluid reaching your gut. Slowed digestion from the medicine itself is usually the bigger factor rather than the weight loss alone.

### What is the best natural laxative for diabetic patients?

There isn't one single "best" option, since the right approach depends on individual health factors, but NHS guidance recommends starting with dietary fibre, adequate fluids and regular activity before considering laxatives. Anyone managing diabetes alongside constipation should discuss laxative choices with a GP or pharmacist, since some products affect blood sugar monitoring or interact with other medicines.

### What is the best laxative for impacted stool?

Impacted stool often needs a different approach to routine constipation and should be assessed by a GP or pharmacist rather than self-treated, since it may require a stronger osmotic laxative or, in some cases, other interventions. Macrogol is commonly used for impaction under medical guidance, as it works by softening stool over a few days.

body:
# GLP-1 Weight Loss Plateau: What 4 Flat Weeks Mean in the UK

![Sketches of scales, calendar and measuring tape](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791462890474_Sketches-of-scales-calendar-and-measuring-tape.jpeg)

A weight loss plateau on GLP-1 treatment is usually a sign your body is stabilising, not proof the medication has stopped working. The right next step is to review your recent pattern against a proper baseline, rather than guessing, and arrange a clinical medicines review or your 6-month check if you haven't had one. Most people need data, not a dose change, to move forward.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - A research benchmark defines a plateau as less than 5% weight change over 12 weeks, sustained afterward; daily fluctuations can exceed a kilogram.
> - Track weight under similar conditions and compare weekly averages, then log food and protein for 7 to 10 days before assuming treatment needs adjustment.
> - Two to three weekly resistance training sessions can help protect lean muscle; add sustainable daily movement and reassess changes after 4 to 12 weeks.
> - At the six month review, clinicians assess continuation against a common threshold of at least 5% weight loss, plus health markers and side effects.
> - Seek prompt medical advice for persistent vomiting, dehydration signs, severe abdominal pain spreading to your back, or low blood sugar symptoms while using diabetes medicines.

***

## Table of Contents

- [What a weight loss plateau is on GLP-1 treatment](#what-a-weight-loss-plateau-is-on-glp-1-treatment)
- [Why plateaus commonly happen with GLP-1 medicines](#why-plateaus-commonly-happen-with-glp-1-medicines)
- [Practical, evidence-led steps to break or manage a plateau](#practical-evidence-led-steps-to-break-or-manage-a-plateau)
- [Other useful measures and progress signals beyond the scales](#other-useful-measures-and-progress-signals-beyond-the-scales)
- [When to contact your prescriber and safety red flags](#when-to-contact-your-prescriber-and-safety-red-flags)
- [How a structured programme supports people through plateaus](#how-a-structured-programme-supports-people-through-plateaus)
- [Normalising plateaus and focusing on long-term gains](#normalising-plateaus-and-focusing-on-long-term-gains)
- [How we can help if you're stalled on GLP-1 treatment](#how-we-can-help-if-youre-stalled-on-glp-1-treatment)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Sources](#sources)

## What a weight loss plateau is on GLP-1 treatment

A plateau is a period where your weight stays broadly flat for several weeks despite continuing treatment as prescribed. Clinical trials use a working definition of less than 5% weight change over a 12-week interval, sustained afterwards, which is a useful benchmark even outside a research setting, [according to post-hoc SURMOUNT analyses](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39800653/).

![What a weight loss plateau is on GLP-1 treatment — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791463001578_What-a-weight-loss-plateau-is-on-GLP-1-treatment-overview-diagram.jpeg)

It helps to separate a genuine plateau from the normal noise of daily weighing. Fluid shifts, food volume, hormonal cycles and even the time of day can move the number on the scale by a kilogram or more without reflecting any real change in body fat. A single flat week means very little. A flat trend across a full month, measured consistently, is a different story.

Several patterns are worth distinguishing:

- A genuine plateau: weight is stable across weekly averages for 4 or more weeks, with no corresponding drop in measurements or how clothes fit.
- Normal fluctuation: day-to-day changes that reverse within a week, often tied to salt intake, hydration or hormonal timing.
- A slowing curve: weight loss continues but more gradually, which is expected as you get closer to a stable, lower weight.

Clinicians commonly use the 6-month mark as a formal review point. At that stage, the question isn't simply "has the scale moved", but whether the treatment is still delivering enough benefit to justify continuing, adjusting the approach, or stepping back to reassess goals. [Regional formulary guidance aligned with NICE](https://southwest.devonformularyguidance.nhs.uk/formulary/chapters/4-central-nervous-system/4-5-drugs-used-in-weight-management) sets out continuation criteria built around this kind of checkpoint, which is one reason that review matters more than any single week's result.

## Why plateaus commonly happen with GLP-1 medicines

Plateaus aren't a sign that something has gone wrong. They're largely a predictable consequence of how these medicines work, how the body responds to weight loss, and how daily habits quietly shift over months of treatment.

**Metabolic adaptation** is the biggest driver. As you lose weight, your body needs fewer calories to maintain itself: a lighter body has a lower resting energy requirement, simply because there's less tissue to support. The deficit that drove early progress gradually shrinks even if your intake hasn't changed, which naturally slows the rate of loss over time.

**Pharmacology plays a role too.** Dose escalation schedules mean the drug's effect builds gradually, and different agents reach steady state and peak appetite suppression at different points. Time to plateau also varies by starting BMI category, which is one reason two people on the same medicine can see quite different trajectories.

**Behavioural drift is easy to miss.** As appetite cues soften, it becomes easy to underestimate portions that have crept back up, or to assume you're eating less than you actually are. Daily movement often falls too, particularly if early weight loss brought more energy and confidence that later settles into a new, lower-activity routine without anyone noticing the shift.

**Medicine-related effects** can also contribute. Delayed gastric emptying, one of the mechanisms behind reduced appetite, can interact with other medicines you take, altering how they're absorbed or how well they're tolerated. This is exactly why a formal medicines review matters when weight has changed substantially, not just a quick chat about the scales.

**A statistic worth holding onto:** most participants treated with tirzepatide in the SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-4 trials reached a weight plateau by around week 72, with the exact timing varying by starting BMI, according to post-hoc trial analyses. That means a flattening curve at this stage of treatment is a documented part of how these medicines typically perform, not an early warning sign.

Causes considering when your progress has stalled:

- Your resting energy needs have genuinely dropped as your body has become lighter.
- Portion sizes or snacking have quietly increased as appetite suppression has eased.
- Daily non-exercise movement has fallen compared with when you started.
- You're on another medicine whose absorption or dosing may need reviewing alongside your GLP-1.

## Practical, evidence-led steps to break or manage a plateau

Before changing anything about your medication, it's worth understanding exactly what's happening day to day. Guesswork rarely helps here, and a short period of honest tracking usually reveals more than another week of frustration.

1. **Audit your intake objectively.** Keep a food log for 7 to 10 days, focus on protein intake at each meal, and check portion sizes against what you think you're eating rather than what you remember.
2. **Prioritise resistance training.** Two to three sessions a week of progressive strength work helps protect lean muscle mass, which supports your resting metabolic rate as body weight falls. Our [guidance on GLP-1 and exercise](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/glp-1-and-exercise) covers how to structure this safely alongside treatment.
3. **Look at non-exercise movement, not just workouts.** Daily steps, standing time and incidental activity often fall as energy improves and life returns to normal; small, sustainable increases here tend to outlast a short burst of extra cardio.
4. **Never adjust your own dose.** Discuss any concerns about effectiveness with your prescriber rather than increasing, decreasing or spacing out doses yourself; they can assess whether dose escalation or a different agent is appropriate for your case.
5. **Request a medicines review.** If you're on other regular medication, ask for a formal check of interactions and absorption, particularly if your weight has changed significantly, [as the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service recommends](https://sps.nhs.uk/articles/considerations-and-interactions-with-glp-1-receptor-agonists/).
6. **Set a short checkpoint, not an open-ended trial.** Give any change (a tracking period, a training adjustment, a nutrition tweak) 4 to 12 weeks before judging it, and be prepared to revert if it isn't helping.

**Pro Tip:** *Weigh yourself at the same time of day, under similar conditions, and judge progress by the weekly average rather than any single reading.*

It's worth saying plainly: self-adjusting your dose or sourcing additional medication outside a prescription is not a safe route to breaking a plateau. [MHRA guidance is explicit](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/glp-1-medicines-for-weight-loss-and-diabetes-what-you-need-to-know) that these are serious medicines, not a cosmetic quick fix, and that they should be obtained and adjusted only through proper prescribing channels. Protecting lean mass matters here too: rapid weight loss without adequate protein and resistance training risks losing muscle alongside fat, which can make a future plateau harder to shift. Our article on [preventing lean mass loss during GLP-1 treatment](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/glp-1-muscle-loss) goes into more detail on how to structure this.

If you're weighing up how different GLP-1 agents compare in terms of appetite suppression and typical response, a [clinical review of tirzepatide versus semaglutide](https://vivoclinic.org/blog/tirzepatide-vs-semaglutide) is a useful starting point for understanding why individual response varies so much between medicines.

## Other useful measures and progress signals beyond the scales

The scale is only one measurement, and it's often the slowest one to reflect real progress. Several other markers tend to move even when your weight has stalled, and they matter more to your long-term health than a single number.

Worth tracking and raising at your next review:

- **Clinical markers:** HbA1c, blood pressure, waist circumference and lipid panels often improve even during a weight plateau, and these are the measures that matter most for long-term health risk.
- **Strength and energy:** noticeable gains in how much you can lift, how far you can walk without fatigue, or how you sleep are real signs of progress.
- **Mood and daily function:** improvements in motivation, food noise and general wellbeing are worth noting, even if they're harder to quantify.
- **Fit and shape:** looser clothing or a smaller waist measurement can show fat loss continuing even when total body weight hasn't moved.

Bring a simple record to your next clinic review: a weight chart showing weekly averages, a short note on energy and sleep, and any measurements you've taken. This gives your prescriber something concrete to work from, rather than a vague sense that "things have stalled".

## When to contact your prescriber and safety red flags

Most plateaus don't need urgent attention, but some situations do, and it helps to know the difference in advance.

Review and stopping rules depend on the medicine and why it was prescribed. [NICE TA875](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-Recommendations) advises considering stopping semaglutide for weight management if less than 5% of the initial weight has been lost after six months of treatment. [Tirzepatide uses a different checkpoint](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-practical-guide-to-using-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-15299628589/chapter/prescribing-reviewing-and-stopping-tirzepatide): six months on the highest tolerated dose, with continuation considered against individual benefits and risks. Do not apply weight-management stopping rules to Ozempic used for diabetes. Agree review dates and treatment changes with your prescriber.

Contact your prescriber promptly, or seek urgent care, if you notice:

- Severe or persistent vomiting that prevents you keeping fluids down.
- Signs of dehydration: dizziness, dark urine, or reduced urination.
- Symptoms suggesting pancreatitis, particularly severe abdominal pain spreading to your back.
- Signs of hypoglycaemia if you're also on other diabetes medication, such as shaking, sweating or confusion.

[MHRA safety updates](https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/glp-1-receptor-agonists-reminder-of-the-potential-side-effects-and-to-be-aware-of-the-potential-for-misuse) document thousands of gastrointestinal adverse event reports linked to these medicines, which is why recognising and reporting unusual symptoms matters. Before any appointment, bring your current medicines list, a simple weight timeline, and notes on any symptoms you've had.

## How a structured programme supports people through plateaus

Practical support can help you record weight trends, food, activity and questions for your prescribing service. A medicines review belongs with your clinician; the timing depends on your medicine, indication and individual circumstances. My Timber does not monitor symptoms or make treatment decisions.

## Normalising plateaus and focusing on long-term gains

Plateaus are a phase, not a failure, and treating them that way changes how people respond to them. People who do best are often those who keep their eye on function and quality of life rather than obsessing over a single number on a Tuesday morning.

The worst response to a stall is a sudden, unsupported change made out of frustration. The better response is a plan, a short checkpoint, and someone to talk it through with.

> *— Matt O’Brien*

## How we can help if you're stalled on GLP-1 treatment

SHIFT provides general information and free practical support through My Timber, Grub, Fit and Life Back. These resources do not replace a clinical assessment or medicine review. Prescribing, dispensing, dose changes and clinical monitoring remain the responsibility of your appropriately regulated healthcare provider. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while its regulated treatment partner is not commissioned.

Arrange a review with your own prescriber if progress has stalled or side effects are troublesome. Do not change a medicine dose yourself.

## FAQ

### How do I break a plateau on GLP-1 medication?

Start with an honest audit of food intake, protein and daily movement before assuming the medication has stopped working. If that doesn't shift things within a few weeks, arrange a medicines review with your prescriber to check interactions, absorption and whether dose adjustment is appropriate, [as NHS pharmacy guidance recommends](https://sps.nhs.uk/articles/considerations-and-interactions-with-glp-1-receptor-agonists/).

### Why have I stopped losing weight on GLP-1 treatment?

Weight loss commonly slows as your resting energy needs fall with a lighter body, which is expected rather than a sign of failure. Behavioural changes such as portion creep or reduced daily movement, and in some cases medicine interactions, also contribute, which is why a review helps identify the specific cause.

### How do I shock my body out of a plateau?

There's no safe way to force rapid change by self-adjusting your dose. The evidence-led approach is a short, structured trial such as increased resistance training or tighter food tracking over 4 to 12 weeks, combined with a clinical medicines review if progress stays flat.

### How long do plateaus typically last during GLP-1 treatment?

Plateaus vary, but post-hoc analyses of the SURMOUNT trials found most participants treated with tirzepatide reached a plateau by around week 72, with timing varying by starting BMI. A flat period at this stage of treatment is a documented part of how the medicine typically performs rather than a sign it has stopped working.

### What happens at a 6-month GLP-1 review?

Review and stopping rules depend on the medicine and why it was prescribed. [NICE TA875](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-Recommendations) advises considering stopping semaglutide for weight management if less than 5% of the initial weight has been lost after six months of treatment. [Tirzepatide uses a different checkpoint](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-practical-guide-to-using-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-15299628589/chapter/prescribing-reviewing-and-stopping-tirzepatide): six months on the highest tolerated dose, with continuation considered against individual benefits and risks. Do not apply weight-management stopping rules to Ozempic used for diabetes. Agree review dates and treatment changes with your prescriber.

# Wegovy eligibility for UK men: NHS BMI rules and the two year cap

![Wegovy eligibility article title card](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791552907638_Wegovy-eligibility-article-title-card.jpeg)

You're likely eligible for Wegovy if your BMI is 35 or above with a weight-related health condition, or 30 to 34.9 with specialist-referral criteria, and you can access it through an NHS specialist weight-management service or a private prescription after a clinician consultation. Treatment runs for a maximum of 2 years, and it's not suitable during pregnancy.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - NICE lowers BMI thresholds by about 2.5 kg/m² for several ethnic groups, while clinicians also consider waist size, health, age, and frailty.
> - NHS prescriptions come through specialist tier 3 or tier 4 services, not usually GPs; local capacity varies, and waiting times have no national figure.
> - Private treatment requires assessment by a registered prescriber and dispensing through a regulated pharmacy; services that skip consultation or hide credentials are red flags.
> - For NHS weight management under NICE TA875, consider stopping if weight loss is below 5% of starting weight after six months of treatment. This recommendation limits treatment to two years; other indications have separate pathways.
> - Wegovy is unsuitable during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and people who could become pregnant are advised to use reliable contraception during treatment.

***

## Table of Contents

- [Who is eligible for Wegovy on the NHS: exact criteria and ethnic adjustments](#who-is-eligible-for-wegovy-on-the-nhs-exact-criteria-and-ethnic-adjustments)
- [How to access Wegovy on the NHS: GP, referral, tiers, waiting lists and pilots](#how-to-access-wegovy-on-the-nhs-gp-referral-tiers-waiting-lists-and-pilots)
- [Private prescription: what a private clinic will check, dispensing and legal safeguards](#private-prescription-what-a-private-clinic-will-check-dispensing-and-legal-safeguards)
- [Treatment length, dosing highlights, stopping rules and side effects you need to know](#treatment-length-dosing-highlights-stopping-rules-and-side-effects-you-need-to-know)
- [What clinicians assess and how monitoring works in specialist services](#what-clinicians-assess-and-how-monitoring-works-in-specialist-services)
- [How we support men through eligibility and treatment](#how-we-support-men-through-eligibility-and-treatment)
- [How we can help you check eligibility and get started](#how-we-can-help-you-check-eligibility-and-get-started)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Sources](#sources)

## Who is eligible for Wegovy on the NHS: exact criteria and ethnic adjustments

[NICE](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/informationforpublic) recommends semaglutide (branded as Wegovy) within specialist weight-management services for adults with a BMI of 35 or above who also have at least one weight-related health condition. Adults with a BMI between 30 and 34.9 can also qualify, but only if they meet the specific criteria set for referral into a specialist service rather than general practice.

The comorbidity requirement matters as much as the BMI figure itself. Common qualifying conditions include:

- Type 2 diabetes or significant risk factors for developing it
- High blood pressure that hasn't responded well to other treatment
- Severe obstructive sleep apnoea
- A need for weight loss before urgent or planned surgery
- Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
- Fertility issues linked to weight where assisted conception is being considered
- Certain genetic conditions associated with obesity

NICE also builds in ethnic adjustments to the BMI thresholds, typically lowering them by around 2.5 kg/m² for people from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African and African-Caribbean backgrounds. This reflects the fact that these groups tend to carry higher health risks at a lower BMI than White European populations, so the standard cut-offs would otherwise under-identify people who could benefit.

BMI alone is a blunt measure. [NHS guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/) notes that clinicians weigh it alongside waist measurements and overall health, which is worth knowing if you're a man with a higher muscle mass wondering why the numbers don't quite tell your story. Most services also set an age floor of 18, and some apply upper age or frailty exclusions depending on local policy.

![BMI waist and health factors in eligibility assessment](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791552983756_BMI-waist-and-health-factors-in-eligibility-assessment.jpeg)

## How to access Wegovy on the NHS: GP, referral, tiers, waiting lists and pilots

Your GP is the starting point, but not the endpoint. GPs rarely issue Wegovy prescriptions directly for weight management. Instead, their job is to assess your history, confirm your BMI and comorbidities, and refer you onward.

1. Book a GP appointment and bring a recent, accurate weight and BMI record.
2. Be ready to discuss any weight-related conditions and previous attempts at structured weight-loss programmes, such as dietitian support or NHS-run courses.
3. Your GP refers you to a specialist tier 3 or tier 4 weight-management service, which is usually hospital-based.
4. The specialist team reviews your case against NICE criteria and decides whether to prescribe.

These specialist services are the only part of the NHS authorised to prescribe Wegovy for weight management, and local [interim policy statements](https://www.southwestlondon.icb.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Interim-Policy-Statement-GLP-1-based-meds.pdf) from integrated care boards explicitly instruct primary care not to prescribe it. Capacity varies a great deal by postcode, and waiting lists at specialist services can be long, something government-backed [pilot schemes](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/new-drugs-pilot-to-tackle-obesity-and-cut-nhs-waiting-lists) are trying to ease through community and digital delivery models. Whether that reaches your area yet depends on local commissioning decisions.

**Pro Tip:** *Ask your GP practice whether your local integrated care board has published its own weight-management referral pathway, since the criteria and paperwork can differ slightly between areas.*

If you want to understand how a GP referral compares with going straight to a specialist route, our [GP versus specialist weight-management guide](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/comparisons/nhs-private/gp-vs-specialist-weight-management) sets out the practical differences.

## Private prescription: what a private clinic will check, dispensing and legal safeguards

Wegovy is a prescription-only medicine in the UK, and it's never legitimately sold over the counter. Going private doesn't bypass the clinical checks, it just changes who performs them and how quickly you can start.

A properly run private pathway includes:

- A consultation with a registered prescriber who reviews your medical history, current medications and relevant risk factors
- A genuine clinical assessment of whether Wegovy is appropriate for you, not just a BMI tick-box
- Dispensing through a regulated pharmacy, never an unregulated website or courier service
- A dose-titration schedule that follows the authorised instructions for the exact Wegovy product. For some adults with obesity, a prescriber may consider 7.2 mg once weekly where appropriate. Do not choose or change a dose yourself.

Many patients care about legitimacy and check who's actually behind a prescription, which is a sensible instinct: MHRA approval updates only cover medicines dispensed through regulated channels, with the dose and monitoring decisions made by a named prescriber. If a service skips the consultation, won't name or show the credentials of the prescriber, or offers to post medication with no clinical review, treat that as a red flag and look elsewhere.

## Treatment length, dosing highlights, stopping rules and side effects you need to know

Weekly Wegovy injections start at a low dose and are increased gradually under prescribing supervision. The standard maintenance dose is 2.4 mg once weekly. For some adults with obesity, a prescriber may consider 7.2 mg once weekly after at least four weeks on 2.4 mg. The maximum is 7.2 mg once weekly. Follow the [UK leaflet for your exact product](https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/13800/pil). Under NICE TA875’s weight-management recommendation, NHS treatment is provided through specialist services for a maximum of two years; other indications and pathways must be considered separately.

Review and stopping rules depend on the medicine and why it was prescribed. [NICE TA875](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-Recommendations) advises considering stopping semaglutide for weight management if less than 5% of the initial weight has been lost after six months of treatment. [Tirzepatide uses a different checkpoint](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-practical-guide-to-using-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-15299628589/chapter/prescribing-reviewing-and-stopping-tirzepatide): six months on the highest tolerated dose, with continuation considered against individual benefits and risks. Do not apply weight-management stopping rules to Ozempic used for diabetes. Agree review dates and treatment changes with your prescriber.

Key safety points to know before starting:

- Wegovy is not suitable during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and reliable contraception is advised for anyone who could become pregnant while treated
- A history of pancreatitis or certain thyroid conditions needs discussing with your prescriber before starting
- Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and fatigue, particularly during dose increases
- Rare but serious risks, including vision changes, should be reported promptly

Any suspected side effect, especially an unexpected or serious one, can and should be reported through the [Yellow Card scheme](https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/), the MHRA's official reporting channel for medicine safety.

## What clinicians assess and how monitoring works in specialist services

Before prescribing, a clinician checks your cardiovascular risk, any history of pancreatitis, your current medications for interactions, and, where relevant, confirms you're not pregnant. This isn't paperwork for its own sake, it's the safety gate that decides whether Wegovy is appropriate for you specifically.

Once you're on treatment, ongoing monitoring typically includes:

- Regular weight checks to track progress against the 6-month benchmark
- Reviews of side effects at each follow-up
- Blood tests where your clinical picture calls for them

**Pro Tip:** *Keep a simple weekly note of your weight and any side effects, it makes follow-up appointments faster and gives your clinician a clearer picture than memory alone.*

Medication is one part of a bigger plan. Specialist services pair it with dietary support, activity guidance and behavioural change work, because the evidence behind Wegovy's results comes from trials where it was used alongside lifestyle support, not instead of it. If the medicine isn't working, or side effects become unmanageable, your team will stop treatment and may report significant reactions via Yellow Card.

## How we support men through eligibility and treatment

SHIFT provides general information and free practical support through My Timber, Grub, Fit and Life Back. These resources do not replace a clinical assessment or medicine review. Prescribing, dispensing, dose changes and clinical monitoring remain the responsibility of your appropriately regulated healthcare provider. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while its regulated treatment partner is not commissioned.

## How we can help you check eligibility and get started

You can use our [Weight-Loss Decision Centre](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/decision-centre) to explore general information and practical support. It does not confirm eligibility or arrange a prescribing consultation. Ask an appropriately regulated provider for an individual assessment. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed.

## FAQ

### What are the NHS eligibility criteria for Wegovy in 2026?

You need a BMI of 35 or above with at least one weight-related health condition, or a BMI of 30 to 34.9 if you meet specialist-referral criteria, under NICE guidance. Lower BMI thresholds, typically around 2.5 kg/m² less, apply for some ethnic groups, and prescribing only happens within specialist tier 3 or tier 4 services.

### What are the NHS criteria for getting Wegovy?

For weight management under NICE TA875, a specialist service assesses BMI, weight-related conditions and suitability; a lower BMI threshold may apply for some ethnic groups. This recommendation limits treatment to two years and advises considering stopping if weight loss is below 5% of starting weight after six months of treatment. Other indications and pathways must be assessed separately.

### Can a GP prescribe Wegovy UK?

GPs generally don't prescribe Wegovy directly for weight management. Instead, NHS guidance and local interim policies point to specialist tier 3 and tier 4 services as the only NHS route, with your GP handling the initial assessment and referral.

### How long is the NHS waiting list for Wegovy?

Waiting times vary significantly by area because specialist service capacity differs between integrated care boards, and demand regularly outstrips places. Government-backed pilot schemes are testing community and digital models to ease this, but there's no single national waiting-time figure to quote.

summary: A plateau can be expected on Ozempic. See when NICE recommends review, what to check before changing treatment, and how food and strength habits may help.
body:
# Ozempic Weight Loss Plateau: UK Six Month Review and Safe Next Steps

![Hand-drawn title card for plateau review](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791635949000_Hand-drawn-title-card-for-plateau-review.jpeg)

A weight loss plateau on Ozempic is common and expected for many people partway through treatment, not a sign that anything has gone wrong. The first two things worth doing are booking a clinician review to check your adherence and safety, and auditing your own habits honestly before touching your dose. Never adjust your dose yourself, and treat any new severe symptoms as urgent.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - A true plateau lasts several weeks, and a semaglutide trial found stalling commonly around weeks 60 to 68, though individual timing varies.
> - Ozempic is a diabetes medicine. Its treatment review depends on diabetes control and individual benefits and risks; do not apply an obesity-treatment stopping rule to it.
> - Prioritize consistent injection storage and timing, adequate protein, and resistance training two or three times weekly; track portions, liquid calories, sleep, stress, and alcohol.
> - Seek urgent care for severe, persistent abdominal pain, especially if it radiates to your back; vomiting, dehydration, and low blood sugar symptoms warrant attention.
> - Stopping semaglutide often leads to weight regain, and the withdrawal trial found continued treatment sustained further loss while placebo switching did not.

***

## Table of Contents

- [What an Ozempic plateau actually is and when it tends to appear](#what-an-ozempic-plateau-actually-is-and-when-it-tends-to-appear)
- [Why plateaus happen: biology and behaviour both play a part](#why-plateaus-happen-biology-and-behaviour-both-play-a-part)
- [Clinical review and reassessment: what your clinician will check](#clinical-review-and-reassessment-what-your-clinician-will-check)
- [Stepwise, evidence-based strategies to try when weight stalls](#stepwise-evidence-based-strategies-to-try-when-weight-stalls)
- [When to contact a clinician urgently and what happens at review](#when-to-contact-a-clinician-urgently-and-what-happens-at-review)
- [Long-term expectations: maintenance, stopping and regain](#long-term-expectations-maintenance-stopping-and-regain)
- [Our view on plateaus and structured support](#our-view-on-plateaus-and-structured-support)
- [How we can help you get past a plateau](#how-we-can-help-you-get-past-a-plateau)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Sources](#sources)

## What an Ozempic plateau actually is and when it tends to appear

A plateau means your weight has stopped falling for several weeks despite sticking to your injections and your usual eating and activity pattern. It is not the same as a single week where the scale does not move. Bodies rarely lose weight in a straight line, so a short stall is normal. A genuine plateau is a sustained flattening over a period extending for several weeks.

Trial evidence gives a rough sense of timing. In a [randomised withdrawal trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33755728/) of weekly semaglutide, continued treatment produced further weight loss compared with switching to placebo, and a plateau commonly appeared around weeks 60 to 68 in that trial setting. That timing will not match everyone, but it shows that stalling later in treatment is built into how the drug tends to behave over time, not a personal failing.

Ozempic is licensed for type 2 diabetes; Wegovy has separate indications and dosing. Evidence about semaglutide for obesity does not make weight loss alone the test of whether Ozempic is working. Ask your prescriber to review your diabetes control, symptoms and individual treatment goals.

![What an Ozempic plateau actually is and when it tends to appear — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791636102485_What-an-Ozempic-plateau-actually-is-and-when-it-tends-to-appear-overview-diagram.jpeg)

## Why plateaus happen: biology and behaviour both play a part

Most plateaus come from a mix of two things: how your body adapts to weight loss, and small shifts in daily habits that creep in without you noticing.

On the biological side, your body needs fewer calories to function once you weigh less, so the same food intake that drove weight loss early on can simply maintain you later. [Reviews of obesity pharmacotherapy](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10674813/) describe this metabolic adaptation alongside a loss of lean muscle mass during weight loss, which further lowers the energy your body burns at rest.

On the behavioural side, appetite suppression can ease slightly as your body adjusts, and small increases in portion size or snacking often slip in unnoticed. Activity levels sometimes drop too, particularly once initial motivation settles into routine.

Medication factors matter as well:

- Missed or delayed doses can quietly reduce the drug's effect week to week.
- Poor injection technique or incorrect storage can affect how well the medicine works.
- Other medicines you take can interact with semaglutide or affect appetite and metabolism independently.

**A plateau doesn't mean the medicine has stopped working. It usually means your body and your medicine have reached a new balance, and something needs to shift to move past it.**

## Clinical review and reassessment: what your clinician will check

Review and stopping rules depend on the medicine and why it was prescribed. [NICE TA875](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-Recommendations) advises considering stopping semaglutide for weight management if less than 5% of the initial weight has been lost after six months of treatment. [Tirzepatide uses a different checkpoint](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-practical-guide-to-using-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-15299628589/chapter/prescribing-reviewing-and-stopping-tirzepatide): six months on the highest tolerated dose, with continuation considered against individual benefits and risks. Do not apply weight-management stopping rules to Ozempic used for diabetes. Agree review dates and treatment changes with your prescriber.

A thorough review usually covers:

- Your dose history and whether you have reached the intended maintenance dose.
- Adherence, including missed doses and injection technique.
- Any medicines started or stopped since you began treatment.
- Safety checks, including symptoms that might point to pancreatitis or problematic blood sugar drops.
- Other health conditions that could be affecting your progress.

The [MHRA's updated safety guidance](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/697a35293c71d838df6bd3fb/DSU_GLP-1s_and_pancreatitis_for_publishing_29-01-26.pdf) strengthened its warnings on acute pancreatitis for GLP-1 medicines, advising anyone with severe, persistent abdominal pain to seek medical attention straight away. A review visit is also the place to raise this if it applies to you.

**Pro Tip:** *Write down your weight trend, any missed doses and new medicines before your appointment. It turns a vague "it's not working" conversation into a specific one your clinician can actually act on.*

Dose changes should only happen under clinical supervision. Semaglutide dosing is titrated carefully, and the [Gov](https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/glp-1-receptor-agonists-reminder-of-the-potential-side-effects-and-to-be-aware-of-the-potential-for-misuse) is explicit that adjustments should be clinician-led, partly because of hypoglycaemia risk in people who are not diabetic.

## Stepwise, evidence-based strategies to try when weight stalls

Before anything else, audit the basics. Missed injections, incorrect storage temperature and inconsistent timing between doses can all blunt the effect of your medicine without any obvious symptom to warn you.

1. **Check your technique and timing first.** Confirm your pen storage, injection site rotation and weekly schedule match the guidance you were given.
2. **Protect your protein intake.** Lean muscle tends to decline during weight loss, and inadequate protein makes that worse, which in turn lowers the calories your body burns at rest, according to [reviews of weight maintenance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10674813/).
3. **Track what you are actually eating and drinking.** Liquid calories from juice, alcohol and flavoured coffees are easy to underestimate, and appetite suppression sometimes masks gradual portion creep.
4. **Add resistance training.** Progressive strength work two or three times a week helps preserve the muscle mass that medication alone will not protect, supporting the energy expenditure that keeps weight loss moving.
5. **Change the stimulus with shorter, harder sessions.** A few weeks of higher-intensity intervals can break a routine your body has adapted to, without needing more total exercise time.
6. **Look at sleep, stress and alcohol together.** Poor sleep and chronic stress are linked with weight gain and harder-to-shift weight through their effect on appetite hormones and cravings, per the [Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health](https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/obesity-prevention-source/obesity-causes/sleep-and-obesity). Alcohol adds calories and can undercut sleep quality on top of that.
7. **Review your medicine timing with food and other prescriptions.** Some interactions and administration habits affect absorption or tolerability in ways worth raising with a clinician rather than guessing at.

**Pro Tip:** *Adding two short strength sessions a week is often more useful during a plateau than adding more cardio. It protects the muscle mass that keeps your metabolism from slowing further.*

If none of these changes shift things within a reasonable window, your clinician might consider a supervised dose adjustment or discuss an alternative licensed weight-management pathway. That decision sits with them, informed by your bloods, symptoms and response so far, never with self-adjustment at home.

## When to contact a clinician urgently and what happens at review

Some symptoms need prompt attention rather than waiting for a scheduled review. The MHRA's strengthened pancreatitis warning and wider drug safety guidance point to a short list of red flags:

- Severe or persistent abdominal pain, particularly radiating to your back.
- Ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea with signs of dehydration, such as dizziness or a dry mouth.
- Symptoms of low blood sugar, including shakiness, sweating or confusion.

A review typically looks at your weight trend over recent weeks, basic bloods where relevant, and whether a referral to specialist weight-management services is appropriate. The likely outcomes are continued monitoring, a supervised change to your treatment, or stopping the medicine if the NICE six-month threshold applies to your case.

## Long-term expectations: maintenance, stopping and regain

Semaglutide appears to work best as an ongoing treatment rather than a short course. The same withdrawal trial that showed plateauing around weeks 60 to 68 also found that people who continued treatment kept losing weight, while those switched to placebo did not maintain the same trajectory.

Stopping the medicine often brings some weight regain, which is why maintenance planning matters as much as the initial weight loss phase. Reviews of obesity pharmacotherapy describe this pattern consistently across potent weight-loss treatments. Ongoing behavioural support, whether or not you remain on medication, tends to matter just as much as the prescription itself.

## Our view on plateaus and structured support

Some approaches are built around the idea that a plateau is a checkpoint, not a failure, and pair clinical review with practical food guidance, achievable movement, and progress tracking so a stall gets caught early rather than drifting for months unnoticed. Men are supported at this stage regardless of where they started treatment, because the honest answer to "why has this stopped working" usually needs a proper look at adherence, habits and safety together, not a guess.

> *— Matt O’Brien*

## How we can help you get past a plateau

SHIFT provides general information and free practical support through My Timber, Grub, Fit and Life Back. These resources do not replace a clinical assessment or medicine review. Prescribing, dispensing, dose changes and clinical monitoring remain the responsibility of your appropriately regulated healthcare provider. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while its regulated treatment partner is not commissioned.

Speak to your own diabetes or prescribing team about a plateau. Supplements are not a substitute for assessment, and SHIFT does not recommend a branded supplement stack as a plateau treatment.

## FAQ

### How do you break a plateau on Ozempic?

Review and stopping rules depend on the medicine and why it was prescribed. [NICE TA875](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-Recommendations) advises considering stopping semaglutide for weight management if less than 5% of the initial weight has been lost after six months of treatment. [Tirzepatide uses a different checkpoint](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-practical-guide-to-using-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-15299628589/chapter/prescribing-reviewing-and-stopping-tirzepatide): six months on the highest tolerated dose, with continuation considered against individual benefits and risks. Do not apply weight-management stopping rules to Ozempic used for diabetes. Agree review dates and treatment changes with your prescriber.

### Why have I stopped losing weight with Ozempic?

Plateaus usually come from a combination of metabolic adaptation, where your body needs fewer calories after weight loss, and small behavioural shifts like slightly larger portions or reduced activity. Missed doses or injection technique issues can also blunt the medicine's effect, so these are worth checking first.

### How to shock your body out of a plateau?

There is no safe way to "shock" your body into losing weight faster, and self-adjusting your dose is not recommended. Short, higher-intensity exercise sessions and adding resistance training can change the stimulus your body is used to, while a clinician review checks whether anything medical needs addressing.

### How can I get Ozempic to start working again?

Ozempic has not usually stopped working outright. An adherence and technique audit, alongside a clinical review of your dose and any new medicines, is the right first step, and any further dose change should only happen under clinical supervision.
